extracted.intended_audience: general readers or students of classic literature (readers of Don Quixote)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of evaluative statements and prescriptive remarks embedded in a chapter of Don Quixote (debates about the truth/value of chivalric books, narrative description, and folk wisdom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed particulars confer appearance of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Books that 'tell us the father, mother, country, kindred, age, place, and the achievements, step by step, and day by day, performed by such a knight or knights' gain the appearance of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote argues that narratives giving precise personal and factual detail make improbable stories seem as credible as historical accounts (he compares denial of Amadis to denying the sun gives light). Used as a rhetorical defense of chivalric romances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid, marvellous imagery delights readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages describing fantastical spectacles (boiling lakes, seven castles, groves, jewelled palaces, damsels, enchanted baths and sumptuous banquets) are presented as supremely delightful to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator/Don Quixote holds that such extravagant, sensory-rich scenes are what fill a reader 'with delight and wonder' and are a key feature of the knight-errant histories that entertain and elevate spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratives should depict moral and knightly virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The life of a knight-errant is said to teach virtues: 'valiant, polite, generous, well-bred, magnanimous, courteous, dauntless, gentle, patient,' and the capacity to bear hardships, imprisonments, and enchantments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote claims that reading/imitating knightly deeds shapes character; thus effective chivalric tales both entertain and provide moral exemplars for readers and protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical relics/supporting artefacts bolster belief in legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention of tangible items (Roland’s horn, Babieca’s saddle, a pin in the king’s armoury) is used as evidence to argue for the existence or historicity of legendary knights and their deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don Quixote uses the presence or reported presence of relics and trophies as a criterion for accepting legendary narratives as true or plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental guidance: present good options and allow choice
rubrics_metrics.description: When a father must choose a spouse for his daughter and suitors are equally qualified, it is recommended to present good candidates and let the daughter choose according to her inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goatherd/narrator explicitly recommends this course as 'worthy of imitation by all fathers who wish to settle their children in life'—an explicit prescriptive social guideline embedded in the tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty as the best protection for young women
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 'no locks, or guards, or bolts that can protect a young girl better than her own modesty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as practical moral advice about safeguarding reputation and virtue; offered as a general maxim rather than procedural instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical squirely advice (comic folk wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sancho Panza's counsel: a knight-errant’s squire should 'eat until he can hold no more' when he has the chance because they may become lost in woods and go without food for days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A piece of pragmatic (and comic) guidance offered within the narrative as a readiness/preparedness maxim for itinerant life; functions as character-based, situational advice rather than formal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom can arise from humble places
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims such as 'the woods breed men of learning, and shepherds’ huts harbour philosophers' and 'they shelter men of experience' propose that rustic or lowly environments produce practical wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative endorsement of the view that experience and common-sense intelligence are not limited to the educated elite; used within the chapter to justify listening to the goatherd's tale.
